A eunuch is a male human being whose testicles have been surgically removed, making him permanently unable to reproduce and, in most cases, unable to engage in sexual activity. Sometimes the operation also removed the penis, but the removal of the testicles alone was the defining characteristic. This procedure is called castration.

That's the biological fact at the heart of the word. Everything else — the history, the roles, the significance — flows from this one physical reality.

To truly understand what a eunuch is, you need to briefly understand what testicles do. Testicles produce testosterone, the primary male sex hormone. Testosterone is responsible for the physical changes a boy goes through during puberty — a deepening voice, facial and body hair, muscle growth, sexual desire, and the ability to father children.

When the testicles are removed before puberty, none of those changes happen fully. The boy's voice remains higher-pitched, his body hair stays sparse, his muscles stay softer, and he never develops a strong sex drive. He also grows unusually tall, because testosterone normally signals the body's bones to stop growing, and without it, the bones keep growing longer.

When castration happened after puberty, some masculine features were already developed and stayed, but the man lost his sex drive and fertility, and his body gradually softened over time.

This biological outcome — a male who is sterile, sexually non-threatening, and physically different from other men — is exactly what made eunuchs so significant throughout history.

People were made into eunuchs for several distinct reasons across different cultures and time periods.

1. To guard and serve in royal harems.
In many powerful empires — Persian, Ottoman, Chinese, Egyptian — rulers kept a "harem," a private quarters where their wives, concubines, and female relatives lived. These women were considered the ruler's exclusive property. No ordinary man could be trusted near them. A eunuch, however, posed no sexual threat, so eunuchs were employed as servants, guards, and managers of these women's quarters. They lived among the women daily and were considered safe precisely because of what had been done to them.

2. To serve as trusted political officials.
Here is one of the most important — and surprising — roles of eunuchs. Because a eunuch could not father children, he could never build his own dynasty or pass power down to a son. A regular ambitious official might scheme to make himself king and put his children on the throne. A eunuch could not. This made eunuchs uniquely "safe" to rulers who feared rivals. As a result, eunuchs were often appointed to extremely powerful government positions — as advisors, ministers, and administrators — because their loyalty could not be divided by family ambition.

In imperial China, this reached extraordinary heights. Eunuchs sometimes effectively ran the entire government, with emperors completely dependent on them. Some Chinese eunuchs became among the most powerful people in the world during their time. The explorer Zheng He, who led China's famous naval expeditions in the early 1400s, was a eunuch.

In the Ottoman Empire, the Chief Black Eunuch — known as the Kizlar Agha — controlled access to the Sultan himself, managed the imperial household, and wielded enormous political influence. The position was one of the most powerful in the entire empire.

3. For religious devotion.
In some ancient religious traditions, men voluntarily castrated themselves as an act of spiritual dedication or worship of certain deities. Priests of the goddess Cybele in ancient Rome are a well-known example. Some early Christian sects also practiced self-castration, interpreting certain religious texts very literally as encouraging men to remove sources of sexual temptation.

4. To preserve a singing voice.
In Europe, roughly from the 1500s to the 1800s, boys who showed exceptional singing ability were sometimes castrated before puberty. This preserved their high, pure vocal range while their lungs and chest grew to adult size, creating an incredibly powerful high-pitched voice that no adult man or woman could match. These singers were called castrati, and they were superstars of the European opera world. The most famous castrato was Farinelli, who performed across Europe to enormous acclaim in the 18th century. The Catholic Church employed castrati in its choirs for centuries. This practice was eventually banned and died out entirely.

5. As punishment or enslavement.
Castration was sometimes used as a punishment for certain crimes (particularly sexual crimes), and enslaved men were sometimes castrated by their captors to make them more controllable and to prevent them from fathering free children.
How Did Someone Become a Eunuch?

The process was almost always irreversible and usually happened in one of a few ways.

Some boys were castrated by their own families, particularly poor families who believed that entering the imperial service as a eunuch was their son's only path to power and a better life. In imperial China, families sometimes made this devastating decision when their sons were very young. In some cases, boys castrated themselves hoping to enter royal service.

Some men were forcibly castrated as prisoners of war, as enslaved people, or as a form of punishment.

Some men made the choice voluntarily for religious reasons or, in the case of castrati, for a musical career.

The procedure was extremely dangerous without modern medicine. Many died from infection or blood loss. Those who survived carried the physical and social consequences for the rest of their lives.
What Was Life Like for Eunuchs?

The experience of being a eunuch varied enormously depending on the era, the culture, and the individual's position.

At the top of the scale, some eunuchs lived lives of extraordinary wealth, influence, and power — managing empires, commanding armies, accumulating vast fortunes. They were feared and respected.

At the bottom, eunuchs were servants with no rights, treated as less than fully human, occupying an ambiguous space in society — considered neither fully male nor female, and often mocked or looked down upon for what they lacked.

Socially, eunuchs existed in a kind of in-between world. They were men in many respects, but they did not fit the expected role of a man in any society — they could not be husbands in the traditional sense, could not father children, and did not have the same social standing as intact males. This exclusion from normal male social life both limited them and, paradoxically, opened certain doors. Because they were seen as "different," they were allowed access to spaces and roles that no regular man could occupy.

The historical practice of creating eunuchs for court service, religious purposes, or musical careers has essentially disappeared from the world. The word "eunuch" today is mostly used in two ways.

First, it appears constantly in historical contexts — when scholars, students, or writers discuss ancient empires, medieval courts, or early modern history. You will encounter the word frequently when reading about the Ottoman Empire, ancient China, ancient Rome and Persia, or the history of opera.

Second, the word is sometimes used figuratively in modern language to describe a man who is seen as powerless, spineless, or ineffectual — someone who has the position or title of authority but none of the actual power or will to act. This usage is considered insulting and derogatory, and carries a strong negative connotation.

It is important to acknowledge that for the vast majority of eunuchs throughout history, this was not a choice freely made as an adult. It was done to children — often very young boys — by their families, by rulers, by captors, or by institutions. By any modern standard, this represents a severe violation of a person's body and autonomy. Many eunuchs suffered enormously, both physically and emotionally. The fact that some rose to great power does not erase the fundamental injustice of what was done to them.

A eunuch is a castrated male — a man or boy whose testicles (and sometimes penis) have been removed, leaving him sterile, sexually non-threatening, and physically altered by the absence of testosterone. Throughout history, eunuchs served as harem guards, trusted political officials, religious figures, and celebrated singers. They occupied a unique and ambiguous place in their societies, sometimes wielding enormous power and sometimes suffering as marginalized outcasts. The deliberate creation of eunuchs is largely a thing of the past, but the word remains important for understanding history, literature, and culture across many civilizations.
